opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think what I value most is how seriously we take the question of measurement. It's easy to say a model is "better," but better at what, and for whom? A lot of my work has been about building evaluations that track things people actually care about, like real professional tasks, rather than only academic benchmarks that get saturated quickly.

The research culture here treats evals as a core part of the work, not an afterthought. When we're training a model, we want a clear picture of where it's improving, where it's falling short, and where it might pose risks. That feedback loop between capabilities research and evaluation is really valuable, because it keeps us honest. If an eval shows the model isn't doing something well, that becomes a research direction.

I also appreciate the willingness to look at hard questions directly. Some evals measure economically useful work, and others measure potentially dangerous capabilities that we want to understand before deployment. Both matter, and it's meaningful to work somewhere that invests in each.

The last thing is the emphasis on grounding things in reality. Bringing in domain experts, people who do the job every day, to define what good output looks like and to grade it makes the results more trustworthy. It also helps us explain progress to the outside world in terms people can relate to, not just a number on a leaderboard.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes improving models on real professional tasks people care about and grounding progress in reality, rather than treating benchmark scores as the goal.

r002.rationale: It does not say OpenAI has published evaluation results when its models were not the best.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think what I value most is that we try to be honest with ourselves about what we actually know versus what we're assuming. It's really easy, when you're building a model, to look at a benchmark score going up and feel good about it. But a number on a leaderboard doesn't tell you whether the model can do the thing you actually care about. So a lot of the work I find meaningful is about building evaluations that are grounded in real tasks, things that real experts do, where you can look at the output and say, "Yes, a professional would accept this," or "No, this would get someone fired."

The other piece is that evaluation and improvement aren't separate activities for us. When you build a good eval, you learn where the model fails, and that feeds directly back into training and into how we think about what the next generation should be able to do. It's a loop. And I think the culture here really values the people who find the uncomfortable results, the places where the model looks great on paper and then falls apart on something a human would find easy. Those findings are treated as valuable, not as bad news to be hidden.

And then there's the safety side, which is inseparable from capability evaluation in my view. If we're going to say a model is safe to deploy, we need to understand what it can do, including the things we'd rather it couldn't. Measuring that rigorously, with the same care we put into measuring the good stuff, is something I think the program takes seriously, and that matters a lot to me.

r001.rationale: The response says leaderboard scores alone do not show whether a model can do the task people care about, and emphasizes evaluations grounded in real tasks and expert standards.

r002.rationale: It discusses valuing uncomfortable evaluation findings, but does not state that OpenAI has published results when its models were not the best.

astra-6.text: What I value is the close connection between improving a model and understanding how well it actually works. Evaluation shouldn’t just give you a score; it should help you see where the model is useful, where it falls short, and what to work on next. That creates a productive feedback loop: you make a change, test your assumptions, and let what you learn guide the next iteration.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluation should reveal where the model is useful and guide improvements, rather than treating a score as sufficient. This conveys usefulness as the aim of improvement.
